Understanding Climate Change Where You Live

You learn what climate change is and how it works, how it shows up in different parts of Nigeria, and how to measure your own household's vulnerability. By the end you have a family climate record, a local seasonal calendar and your top three vulnerabilities.
Weather, climate and the greenhouse effect: what is really changing

People often say "the weather has changed". What they usually mean is that the **climate** has changed. The two words are different, and knowing the difference helps you read news, forecasts and your own experience correctly. **Weather** is what the sky and air are doing today or this week: rain this afternoon, a hot night, harmattan dust on Friday. **Climate** is the usual pattern of weather in a place over many years: when the rains normally start, how hot March normally is, how long the dry season normally lasts.

How many years make a climate? The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations body for weather and climate, uses **30-year averages**, called climate normals, for example 1991 to 2020. One late rainy season is weather. Rains that arrive later, on average, across ten, twenty or thirty years show a change in climate.
A sun partly hidden behind a rain cloud
Weather is today's sun and rain; climate is the pattern those days make over many years.
The greenhouse effect in plain words

Sunlight passes through the air and warms the ground, the sea and our roofs. The warm ground then gives off heat back towards the sky. Some gases in the air, called **greenhouse gases**, hold part of that heat in, like a thick wrapper on a sleeping baby. Without them the Earth would be too cold for life. The problem is that people have added much more of these gases, so more heat is held in and the whole planet is warming.

Each step follows from the one before: adding gases at step three is what pushes temperatures up.

According to the United Nations, human activities have been the main driver of climate change since the 1800s, mainly through burning **fossil fuels**: coal, oil and gas. The UN reports that the average temperature of the Earth's surface is now about **1.4°C warmer** than in the late 1800s. That sounds small, but it is an average over the whole planet, day and night, land and sea. A small rise in the average brings many more very hot days and heavier downpours.

Africa as a whole has added a small share of these gases compared with richer, industrialised regions, yet many African families feel the effects sharply because so much depends on rain: farming, water from wells and streams, and food prices in the market. That is why this course puts most of its weight on **coping and adapting**, while still showing the small cuts in emissions that also save money.
Three words you will use all through this course
**Adaptation**: changing how we live and work to reduce harm from a changing climate. For example, storing more water before the dry season or moving a shop's goods off the floor in the rainy season.
**Mitigation**: reducing the greenhouse gases we add, or taking them back out of the air. For example, using less charcoal or planting and protecting trees.
**Resilience**: the ability of a household or community to absorb a shock, such as a flood or a heatwave, recover quickly and come back stronger rather than poorer.
Worked example: is it weather or climate?

For example, Amina in a village near Bauchi has a family notebook in which her father wrote the date of the first rain good enough for planting each year. She counts days from 1 April (1 April = day 1) to compare years.
Years 2016 to 2020: day 12 (12 April), day 25 (25 April), day 38 (8 May), day 19 (19 April), day 30 (30 April).
Average for these five years: (12 + 25 + 38 + 19 + 30) / 5 = 124 / 5 = 24.8, about day 25, which is 25 April.
Years 2021 to 2025: day 44 (14 May), day 33 (3 May), day 51 (21 May), day 40 (10 May), day 58 (28 May).
Average for these five years: (44 + 33 + 51 + 40 + 58) / 5 = 226 / 5 = 45.2, about day 45, which is 15 May.
Difference between the two averages: 45 - 25 = 20 days later.
She notices that 2018 (8 May) was late on its own, but the years after it went back to April. One late year is weather. A whole run of later years is a sign of a shifting pattern.

In her family's record, planting rains now arrive about 20 days later on average than five to ten years ago. Ten years is still shorter than WMO's 30-year normal, so Amina treats it as a strong local warning sign to plan around, not as final proof, and she keeps recording every year.
Your own records count

Official weather stations are far apart. A family notebook with dates of first rains, floods, very hot spells and harvests is valuable local evidence. Start one this week, even if you can only fill in what you remember from last year.

Keep three ideas from this lesson: climate is the long average, not one bad day; extra greenhouse gases from human activity are warming the planet; and your household can respond in two ways at once, by adapting to what is already happening and by cutting waste that adds to the problem.

A false start

A **false start** is when early rains arrive, farmers plant, and then a long dry spell kills the seedlings. Many farmers now wait for two or three good rains and moist soil before planting. Your community's experience of false starts is important climate information.
The "then and now" seasonal calendar

Official data covers big areas. Older residents can tell you what has changed on your street or farm. A **seasonal calendar** is a simple chart of the twelve months on which people mark when things usually happen. You make two rows: **Then** (about 20 to 30 years ago) and **Now** (the last five years). Then you compare.
Invite three to six older people, including at least two women, for about 45 minutes. A women's meeting, church or mosque group, or market association works well.
Draw the twelve months across a large sheet of paper, or on the ground with sticks.
For the Then row, ask: When did the rains usually start? When did they end? When was the hottest time? When was water hardest to get? When was food scarce before harvest?
Mark each answer with a symbol: a drop for rain, a sun for heat, an empty pot for water shortage, an empty basket for hunger.
Repeat the same questions for the Now row.
Ask what people do differently now because of the changes. Write down every answer, including ones you disagree with.

Trend or one-off?

Memory can be strong for dramatic years and weak for ordinary ones. To avoid mistakes, check that **several people agree**, ask for **examples with years** ("the year of the big flood was the year my son was born"), and compare with any written records, like Amina's notebook in Lesson 1, or with official information. If only one person remembers a change, write it down but mark it as "to check".
Respect every answer

Some elders explain changes through faith or tradition. Listen respectfully and record what they say. You are collecting observations of what changed and when; you do not need to argue about causes during the session.

Two families can live on the same street, face the same dry spell, and come out very differently. One loses income and pulls a child out of school; the other has a hard month and recovers. The difference is **vulnerability**. In this course, vulnerability means how prone you are to harm. It depends on how **sensitive** you are and how much **capacity** you have to cope and adapt. Add **exposure**, whether the hazard reaches you at all, and you have a simple tool for your own household.
The three parts
**Exposure**: does the climate hazard reach this part of your life? A shop on low ground is exposed to flooding; one on a hill is less exposed.
**Sensitivity**: if it reaches you, how badly does it hurt? A family whose only income is a rain-fed maize farm is very sensitive to a late rainy season. A salaried worker is less sensitive.
**Adaptive capacity**: what do you have that helps you cope and adjust? Savings, a second income, stored water, a strong group, information, skills and good health all add capacity.

Your home, water, food, income and health each carry their own climate risks.

Capacity gap: 1 if you are well prepared, 3 if you have little to fall back on. Add the three scores. Totals run from 3 to 9. The higher the total, the more vulnerable that area is.

Ngozi's top three vulnerabilities are: (1) flood damage to shop stock, (2) heat stress for her elderly mother at night, and (3) food price rises after poor harvests. She will tackle the shop first, because it scored highest and also feeds the family.

Memories and elders' stories show the big picture. A daily log shows exactly what is happening this season. With a plastic container, a ruler and two minutes each morning, you can measure rainfall in **millimetres (mm)**, the same unit used by weather services. Over a few seasons, your log becomes a record your community can trust.
A grey cloud with falling rain
Each millimetre of rain you record adds to a local record no weather station far away can give you.
What 1 mm of rain means

Rainfall is measured as the depth of water that would stand on flat ground if none soaked in, ran off or dried up. If rain fills a straight-sided container to 12 mm deep, then 12 mm of rain fell. The width of the container does not matter, as long as the sides are straight up and down and the bottom is flat. A wider container simply catches more water, spread over a wider base, so the depth is the same.
Two ways to build a gauge

**Straight-sided gauge (simplest):** a clear plastic jar or container with straight sides and a flat bottom, at least 10 cm wide. Measure the water depth with a ruler held upright from the inside bottom. Read in millimetres.

**Funnel gauge (better for small rains):** a funnel on top of a bottle catches rain over the funnel's mouth and keeps it from evaporating. Measure the water in millilitres (ml) with a kitchen measuring jug or marked feeding bottle, then convert to mm with the formula below.

The funnel formula: **rain in mm = water in ml ÷ funnel opening area in square centimetres × 10**. Find the area with **3.14 × radius × radius**, where the radius is half the width across the funnel's mouth. This works because 1 ml is 1 cubic centimetre, so ml ÷ area gives depth in centimetres, and × 10 turns centimetres into millimetres.
Worked example: reading a funnel gauge
For example, Hadiza in Minna uses a funnel 15 cm across its mouth fitted into a 1.5-litre bottle. After a night storm she pours the water into a measuring jug.
Radius = 15 ÷ 2 = 7.5 cm.
Funnel area = 3.14 × 7.5 × 7.5 = 176.6 square centimetres (rounded).
Water collected: 530 ml.
She writes "14 June, 30 mm, storm at night" in her log and empties the bottle.
A 30 mm night storm is a heavy rain for one night. When she checks her log at the end of the season, she can count how many nights like this occurred and whether they are becoming more common.
Placing and reading the gauge
Put the gauge in an open place, away from roofs, walls and trees. A simple rule: keep it at least as far from any obstacle as that obstacle is tall.
Fix it firmly so wind, goats or children cannot knock it over: tie it to a short post or set it in a tin of sand, with the top about 30 cm above the ground to avoid splashes.
Read it at the same time every morning, for example 7 am, and record the rain that fell over the last 24 hours.
Empty and dry it after every reading. Cover the opening of any stored water and never leave water standing, so mosquitoes cannot breed.
Write 0 on dry days. A zero is a reading too, and dry runs are as important as rainy days.
Adding temperature

A simple indoor and outdoor thermometer from a pharmacy or electronics shop lets you record heat. Read it in the shade, never in direct sun, at the same time each day, such as 3 pm, the hottest part of most days. Write both outdoor shade temperature and the temperature inside your sleeping room at bedtime. These readings will be used in the next lesson on heat.
Turning a month of readings into information

At the end of each month, work out three numbers: the **total rainfall** (add all readings), the number of **rainy days** (for your log, count a day as rainy if 1 mm or more fell), and the **longest dry run** (the most days in a row with less than 1 mm). Those three numbers tell you more than the total alone.

Worked example: Hadiza's June summary

For example, Hadiza's June log has 30 daily readings. The days with rain were: 2 June 12 mm, 5 June 3 mm, 12 June 25 mm, 13 June 8 mm, 16 June 0.5 mm, 18 June 14 mm, 26 June 30 mm, 27 June 6 mm, 30 June 2 mm. All other days were 0.

Dry runs: 19 to 25 June is 7 days in a row with no rain. 6 to 11 June is 6 days. The longest dry run is 7 days.
She compares this with her notes from last June and with the dry spell warning in the seasonal forecast for her state.
June had about 100 mm of rain but only 8 rainy days and a 7-day dry run in the middle of the month. For her vegetable plot she now knows to mulch and water during runs of more than five dry days.
Linking your log to the official seasonal forecast

The Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet) publishes a Seasonal Climate Prediction early each year. Four of its terms are worth knowing. **Onset**: the expected start of the rainy season. **Cessation**: the expected end. **Length of season**: the days between onset and cessation. **Dry spell**: a run of dry days within the rainy season. When you write your own onset date, cessation date and longest dry runs each year, you can check how well the forecast matched your area, and build your community's trust in using it.
Share the work
A women's group can run one gauge and take turns reading it, with one notebook kept by the secretary. Post the monthly summary in your group's WhatsApp so everyone sees it.

Floods are easy to see. Heat is quieter, but it is also dangerous. As the planet warms, very hot days and hot nights become more common. The World Health Organization (WHO) warns that heatstroke is a medical emergency, and that some groups are at much higher risk. Women are often among them, for example when cooking indoors over a fire in hot weather.
A face red and sweating from heat
Heat illness can come on quietly, so learn the signs before the hot season starts.
Who is most at risk
**Older people**, especially over 65, as WHO highlights. Their bodies sense thirst and heat less well.
**Babies and young children**, who heat up quickly and depend on adults for water and shade.
**Pregnant women**.
**People with long-term illnesses** such as heart disease, diabetes, kidney disease or breathing problems, and people with disabilities who may not be able to move to a cooler place alone.
**Outdoor workers**: farmers, market traders, hawkers, okada riders, builders.
**Families in hot, crowded housing** with little airflow, such as rooms with metal roofs and one small window.
WHO's personal advice in hot weather
Avoid going outside and doing hard physical work during the hottest time of the day.
Drink water regularly. WHO suggests about 1 cup of water per hour and at least 2 to 3 litres per day. Do not wait until you feel thirsty.
Check regularly on vulnerable people around you, especially those over 65.
Pay attention to alerts and advice from local authorities during hot spells.

Keeping the home cooler for little money

Use a damp cloth on the neck and wrists, and cool (not icy) baths or sponging before sleep.
Generators on hot nights

Many families run a generator at night for a fan. Never run a generator indoors, on a closed veranda or near a window or door. Its exhaust contains carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell, which can kill sleeping people.
Inclusion: a heat check rota

The people most at risk are often the least able to ask for help. A **heat check rota** gives each volunteer a short list of named neighbours to visit or call during a hot spell, at a fixed time, with a simple checklist: Do they have water within reach? Are they in the coolest place? Any danger signs? Who will they call if they feel unwell?
Worked example: planning a heat check rota

For example, Kemi's women's group in a Kano neighbourhood lists 14 people at high risk: 9 older people living alone or with only children, 3 pregnant women and 2 people with disabilities. Five members volunteer.

Good intentions do not prove that anything changed. **Measuring** does. In this lesson you choose a few simple indicators, record where you start (the **baseline**), make one change, and measure again. The example focuses on cooking fuel, because it touches three things at once: money, health and greenhouse gases.
A person standing beside a rising bar chart

Why the kitchen matters

WHO reports that about 2.1 billion people worldwide cook with open fires or inefficient stoves using kerosene, wood, charcoal, dung, crop waste or coal. The smoke causes heart disease, stroke, lung infections and lung disease, and WHO notes that women and children, who usually cook and collect firewood, bear the greatest health burden. Using less wood and charcoal also means fewer trees cut and less money spent.

WHO counts these as **clean** cooking options: solar, electricity, biogas, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG, cooking gas), natural gas, alcohol fuels, and biomass stoves that meet WHO's emission targets. If you cannot switch fully yet, using less charcoal or wood with a better stove and good habits is still a step forward.
Habits that cut fuel use
Keep a lid on the pot. Food boils faster and uses less fuel.
Soak beans and hard grains for several hours before cooking.
Use dry wood or charcoal and keep the stove sheltered from wind.
Turn down the heat once food boils: a gentle simmer cooks just as well.

**Retained-heat cooking**: bring a pot of beans, rice or stew to the boil, then place the closed pot in an insulated basket or a box packed with cloths or dry grass. It keeps cooking slowly with no extra fuel. Reheat to boiling before serving if it has cooled.
Smoke and fire safety

Cook in a well-ventilated place, keep babies and young children away from smoke and hot pots, and never bring a burning or glowing charcoal stove into a closed room, because charcoal also produces carbon monoxide. Keep a bucket of sand or water nearby when cooking with fire.

Worked example: did the retained-heat basket save charcoal?

For example, Funke in Ibadan cooks for six people with charcoal. She weighs the charcoal she uses each week for four weeks, then starts using a lid on every pot and a retained-heat basket for beans and stews, and weighs again for four weeks. For this example she pays about ₦700 per kg of charcoal; prices vary by place and season.
Before: 9, 8.5, 9.5 and 9 kg. Average = (9 + 8.5 + 9.5 + 9) ÷ 4 = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 kg per week.
After: 7, 6.5, 7 and 6.5 kg. Average = 27 ÷ 4 = 6.75 kg per week.
Saving: 9 - 6.75 = 2.25 kg per week.
Percentage change: 2.25 ÷ 9 × 100 = 25% less charcoal.
Money saved: 2.25 × ₦700 = about ₦1,575 per week; over 52 weeks about ₦81,900 a year at that price.

In Funke's own kitchen, the lid and basket cut charcoal use by a quarter. She keeps the practice, shows her neighbours her notebook, and starts saving the weekly difference towards a two-burner gas cooker.

If a number did not move, ask why. Was it a festival week with extra cooking? Did the charcoal quality change? Record the reason next to the number. Some of the best climate actions are also the oldest: planting and caring for trees, and keeping water flowing where it should. These are called **nature-based solutions** because they use living things and natural processes to protect people. They work for adaptation and mitigation at the same time: a tree shades a compound today and takes carbon dioxide out of the air as it grows.
A person relaxing among trees and plants
Trees around homes, schools and markets give shade, hold soil and store carbon.
What trees and clear drains do
**Shade and cooling**: a shade tree near a house, school or market stall makes the space under it cooler, which helps the heat-sensitive people from Module 2.
**Holding soil**: roots bind the soil, and leaves soften heavy raindrops, so less soil washes away. Planting and protecting vegetation is a key part of controlling erosion around gullies and slopes.
**Windbreaks**: rows of trees slow dry winds and dust, which matters in the north during harmattan.

**Clear drains**: in towns, a great deal of flooding after heavy rain happens because drains are blocked with plastic bags, bottles and other waste. Water that cannot flow away rises into streets, shops and homes.
Planting so trees survive
Planting a seedling takes ten minutes; keeping it alive takes two years. Many planting days fail because nobody waters or protects the young trees. Plan for care from the start.

Choose the right tree for the place and purpose. Ask your State Ministry of Environment, the state forestry office or a local nursery which species grow well in your zone and suit shade, fruit or erosion control.
Plant at the start of the rainy season, once the soil is properly moist, so roots establish before the dry season.
Dig a hole about twice as wide as the root ball. Remove the polythene bag carefully without breaking the soil around the roots.
Set the seedling at the same depth it was in the bag, fill with soil, press firmly and water well.
Mulch around the base with dry leaves or grass, leaving a small gap at the stem.
Protect it from goats and people with a ring of sticks, an old basket or a thorny branch.
Assign each tree to a named caretaker who waters it during dry spells and the first dry season.

Worked example: counting tree survival

For example, Blessing's women's group plants 60 shade and fruit seedlings around a primary school in Jos, with 12 members each caring for 5 trees. For this example seedlings cost about ₦300 each at a local nursery; prices vary.
Cost of seedlings: 60 × ₦300 = about ₦18,000.
After three months, they count 42 living trees.
Survival rate: 42 ÷ 60 × 100 = 70%.
Trees lost: 60 - 42 = 18. Most losses were on the side next to the football field, where children trampled them.
Replacement cost: 18 × ₦300 = about ₦5,400. They replant at the next rains and add stick rings on that side.
Blessing's group learns that protection was the weak point, not watering. They record the survival rate and the reason, and set a target of at least 85% survival for the replanted trees.
A safe drain clean-up

Drain clearing works best before the heavy rains and as a regular routine, not only after a flood. Talk to your local government area's sanitation or environment office first: they may lend tools, arrange waste collection and tell you which drains are their responsibility.
Protect the people doing the work

Wear thick gloves and boots, cover cuts, and do not let children help in drains. Never enter a drain or gutter during rain or when water is flowing. Lift heavy slabs with several people and proper tools. Wash hands well with soap and water afterwards. Waste from drains can carry germs and sharp objects, so bag it and arrange collection; do not burn it, because burning plastic gives off harmful smoke.

Prevention matters more than clearing. Agree with traders and households on where waste goes, and ask the LGA about regular collection. Some groups also sort clean plastic bottles and sachets for local recyclers who buy them, which can turn a cost into a small income.
Start where people already gather
A school, market, church, mosque or health centre gives you a place everyone uses, a group already organised, and a reason for others to help look after the trees or drains.

What someone may say
A respectful reply
"It is just a bad year, things will go back to normal."
"Maybe. Let us check our records. If the change keeps showing year after year, it is safer to plan for it."
"Climate change is a problem for rich countries."
"They have produced more of the gases, but we are already feeling the effects here: later rains, hotter days. Preparing protects our own families."

Who to partner with

Nigeria's **Climate Change Act, 2021** established the **National Council on Climate Change (NCCC)** as the apex body for climate matters in the country. Most practical help, though, comes from people closer to you.
**State Ministry of Environment and the LGA environment or sanitation office**: waste collection, drain clearing, tree planting programmes.
**Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) extension workers**: advice on crops and seasons for farming families.
**Primary health centre staff**: support for heat safety messages and the heat check rota.
**NiMet**: the seasonal forecast and weather warnings to share with your group.
**Schools, religious groups, market associations and cooperatives**: places, people and trust.
**Registered NGOs working on environment or women's livelihoods in your state**: check they are genuine before sharing any personal data or money.
Making a specific request

Partners respond better to a clear, small, specific request than to "please help us with climate change". Say who you are, what you have already done, exactly what you need, for how many people, and by when.
Introduce your group and its members in one sentence.
Show what you have already done, with numbers: "We planted 60 trees; 42 survived."
State the exact request: "Can your office supply 20 replacement seedlings and stick guards before 15 May?"
Say what you will do in return: "We will water them and send you a survival count after three months."
Give a contact name and phone number, and follow up within one week.
Make communication two-way

Partnerships last longer when information flows in both directions. Do not only receive forecasts and advice: send back what your community observes. A monthly message to your extension worker or LGA environment officer with your rain log summary (total rain, rainy days, longest dry run), any flooding of streets or drains, and how many people your heat rota reached gives them local evidence they rarely have. Keep the message short, with dates and numbers, and keep copies. Over a year, these reports show partners that your group is organised and reliable, which makes the next request easier to grant.
Watch for scams

Be careful of anyone who asks your group to pay a fee to receive "climate grants" or "green funds". Genuine agencies do not ask for payment through personal accounts. Verify any offer directly with the agency's official office before sharing money or members' details.

Worked example: Rahila's project summary

For example, Rahila lives in Lafia and sells pepper and tomatoes. Her top vulnerability in Module 1 was income (score 9): heavy rain flooded her stall, and hot afternoons made her and two older traders beside her unwell.

This is the video for module one of Climate Awareness and Community Resilience.
Why this matters
What you will be able to do
Tell weather and climate apart
Explain the greenhouse effect in plain words

Find your household's top three vulnerabilities
People often say the weather has changed. What they usually mean is that the climate has changed.
Weather is what the sky is doing today or this week. Climate is the usual pattern over many years. The World Meteorological Organization uses 30-year averages, for example 1991 to 2020.
In this video you will learn why the climate is changing, how to read the signs, and where your family is most at risk.
How it works
The ground gives off heat
Greenhouse gases trap some heat
The UN reports the Earth is about 1.4°C warmer than the late 1800s.
Sunlight passes through the air and warms the ground. The warm ground gives off heat back towards the sky.
Some gases, called greenhouse gases, hold part of that heat in, like a thick wrapper on a sleeping baby.
But people have added much more of these gases, mainly by burning coal, oil and gas, and by cutting down forests. So more heat is held in, and the whole planet is warming.
That sounds small, but it is an average over the whole planet. A small rise brings many more very hot days and heavier downpours.
Key words
Three words for the whole course
Changing how we live and work to reduce harm, like storing water before the dry season.
Reducing the gases we add, like using less charcoal or planting and protecting trees.
Absorbing a shock like a flood, recovering quickly, and coming back stronger, not poorer.
Adaptation means changing how we live and work to reduce harm, like moving shop goods off the floor in the rainy season.
Mitigation means reducing the gases we add. For example, using less charcoal, or planting trees.
Resilience is the ability of a household to absorb a shock, recover quickly, and come back stronger rather than poorer.
Worked example
Amina: is it weather or climate?
Her father wrote the first planting rain each year
2016 to 2020: average about 25 April
2021 to 2025: average about 15 May
About 20 days later on average
One late year is weather; a run of years is a pattern
Amina lives in a village near Bauchi. Her family notebook has the date of the first rain good enough for planting, every year.
She averages five years at a time. From 2016 to 2020, the planting rains came on average around 25 April. From 2021 to 2025, around 15 May.
So the rains now arrive about 20 days later on average.
One late year, like 2018, is weather. A whole run of later years is a sign of a shifting pattern.
Ten years is still shorter than 30, so she treats it as a strong warning sign and keeps recording.
Local evidence
Run a then-and-now seasonal calendar
Invite three to six elders, at least two women
Draw twelve months on paper or the ground
Then row: rains, heat, water and food shortages
Now row: the same questions for recent years
Count the shift in months
Trust a change more when several people agree and can name years.
Older residents can tell you what has changed on your street or farm. Invite three to six of them, including at least two women, and draw the twelve months.
In the Then row, about 20 to 30 years ago, mark when the rains started and ended, the hottest time, and when water and food were hardest to get.
Then ask the same questions for the last five years.
For example, in Esther's community in Benue, the rainy season went from about 6.5 months to about 5. That is about 1.5 months shorter.
Memory is strong for dramatic years. If only one person remembers a change, write it down, but mark it to check.
Your household
Three parts of vulnerability
Exposure: does the hazard reach you?
Sensitivity: how badly does it hurt?
Capacity gap: how little you can fall back on
Score each from 1 to 3, total 3 to 9
Exposure asks whether the hazard reaches you at all. A shop on low ground is exposed to flooding.
Sensitivity asks how badly it hurts. A family that depends only on a rain-fed maize farm is very sensitive to late rains.
Capacity is what helps you cope: savings, stored water, a strong group, skills and good health.
Score water, food, income, health and housing from 1 to 3 on each part. Add them. The higher the total, the more vulnerable that area is.
Ngozi scores her household
Income 9: shop stock beside a drain that floods
Health 8: hot nights for her mother, aged 70
Food 7: all food is bought
Quick win: raise stock off the floor
Clear the drain and start a small saving
Score what is true today, not what you plan to do.
Ngozi sells provisions in Onitsha. Her shop scored 9, because her goods sit on the floor beside a drain that overflows. Heat for her elderly mother scored 8, and food prices 7.
Cheap actions lower a score fast. She will raise her goods on pallets or blocks before the rains, clear the drain with her neighbours, and save a little each week in her ajo group.
An honest score of 9 that leads to action protects your family more than a hopeful 5 that hides the problem.
Key points
Remember
Climate is the long average, not one bad day
Extra greenhouse gases are warming the planet
Elders and family records are real evidence
Exposure, sensitivity and capacity make vulnerability
Act first on your highest score

To remember. Climate is the long average, not one bad day. Extra greenhouse gases from human activity are warming the planet. Your family records and your elders are real evidence. And act first where your score is highest.

Why this matters

Memories show the big picture. A daily log shows exactly what is happening this season, in the unit weather services use.
You will also learn to protect the people most at risk from heat, and to measure whether your household actions really work.
Rain gauge
Build, place and read your gauge
Straight-sided clear jar, at least 10 cm wide
Open place, away from roofs, walls and trees
Fix it firmly, top about 30 cm above ground
Read at the same time every morning
Write 0 on dry days
Empty the gauge after every reading so mosquitoes cannot breed.
Use a clear jar with straight sides and a flat bottom. Hold a ruler upright from the inside bottom and read the depth in millimetres. The width does not matter, as long as the sides are straight.
Keep it at least as far from any obstacle as that obstacle is tall.
Tie it to a short post or set it in a tin of sand, so wind, goats or children cannot knock it over.
Read it at the same time each morning, for example 7 am. On dry days, write zero. A zero is a reading too.
Then empty and dry it. Never leave water standing.
Worked example
Hadiza's June in three numbers
Total rain: 100.5 mm
Rainy days of 1 mm or more: 8
Longest dry run: 7 days
Action: mulch and water in long dry runs
At the end of each month, work out three numbers. Hadiza in Minna added all her June readings: 100.5 millimetres.
She counted rainy days, only days with 1 millimetre or more. That gave 8.
And her longest dry run was 7 days in a row, in the middle of the month.
So she now knows to mulch and water her vegetables during runs of more than five dry days.
Heat
Who is most at risk from heat
Older people, especially over 65
Babies, young children and pregnant women
People with long-term illness or disability
Outdoor workers: farmers, traders, okada riders
Families in hot, crowded rooms
Heat is quieter than floods, but it is dangerous. Older people, especially over 65, feel thirst and heat less well.
Babies heat up quickly. Pregnant women, people with long-term illness, and people who cannot move to a cooler place alone are also at higher risk.
So are outdoor workers, and families in rooms with metal roofs and one small window.
WHO advises avoiding hard work in the hottest time of day, and drinking water regularly, about 2 to 3 litres a day, before you feel thirsty.
First aid
Dizzy, headache, heavy sweating. Move to shade, give sips of water, sponge and fan.
Hot skin, confusion, fits, collapse. Get help at once or call 112. Cool with water and fan.
Lay them on their side, keep checking breathing. No drinks if not fully awake.

Heat exhaustion looks like tiredness, dizziness, headache and heavy sweating. Move the person to a cool, shady place, give water to sip, and sponge and fan the skin. If they are not better within about 30 minutes, treat it as heatstroke.
Heatstroke is a medical emergency. Signs include hot skin, confusion, fits or collapse. Get emergency help at once, or call 112, and keep cooling them while you wait.

If the person becomes unconscious, lay them on their side and keep checking their breathing. Never give drinks to someone who is not fully awake, and never give medicines without a health worker's advice.
Cooler home
Keep the home cool and safe
Do
Shade sunny windows by day
Open opposite windows at night
Cook outside or very early
Coolest room for the most at risk
Never
Run a generator indoors
Put a generator near a window or door
Bring a glowing charcoal stove inside
Close curtains or hang a damp cloth on the sunny side by day, and let air flow through at night. Cook outside, and let an older relative or a baby sleep in the coolest room.

Never run a generator indoors, on a closed veranda, or near a window or door. And never bring a glowing charcoal stove into a closed room. Both give off carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell, which can kill sleeping people.
Did Funke's basket save charcoal?
For example, Funke in Ibadan cooks for six people with charcoal.
Charcoal price per kg
Saved per week (2.25 kg)
Saved over 52 weeks
Naira prices are approximate and vary by place.
Funke weighed her charcoal for four weeks first. That is her baseline: 9 kg a week on average.
Then she made one change. A lid on every pot, and a retained-heat basket, where a boiling pot keeps cooking in a box packed with cloths. Four weeks later, she used 6.75 kg a week.
She pays about 700 naira per kg, though prices vary.
She saves 2.25 kg a week. That is 25% less charcoal, and about 1,575 naira a week.
Over 52 weeks, that is about 81,900 naira. She is saving the difference towards a gas cooker.
Measure a baseline first, change one thing at a time, and compare ordinary weeks with ordinary weeks.

Remember
Read the gauge daily, record zeros, empty it
Monthly: total rain, rainy days, longest dry run

Baseline first, one change, then measure again

To remember. Read your gauge every day and record zeros. Sum up each month in three numbers. Treat heatstroke as an emergency. Never run a generator or charcoal stove indoors. And measure a baseline before you change anything.

Why this matters
From knowledge to visible action
Plant trees that actually survive
Clear drains safely before the rains
Explain climate change in ten minutes
Finish your project with an honest 90-day plan
Some of the best climate actions are also the oldest: caring for trees and keeping water flowing. A tree shades a compound today and takes carbon dioxide out of the air as it grows.
In this video you will plan that action, talk about it clearly, find partners, and build your capstone project.
Step by step
Ask a nursery or forestry office which trees suit you
Plant at early rains, once the soil is moist
Hole twice as wide as the root ball, same depth
Mulch, and protect with a ring of sticks
Give every tree a named caretaker
Planting takes ten minutes. Keeping a tree alive takes two years.
Choose the right tree for your zone and purpose: shade, fruit or erosion control. Ask a local nursery or the state forestry office.
Dig a hole about twice as wide as the root ball. Remove the polythene bag carefully, set the seedling at the same depth, press firmly and water well.
Mulch with dry leaves, protect it from goats and people, and give each tree a named caretaker who waters it through the first dry season.
Many planting days fail because nobody waters or protects the young trees. Plan for care from the start.
Worked example
Counting tree survival
For example, Blessing's women's group plants 60 seedlings around a school in Jos.
One seedling
60 seedlings
Replacing 18 lost trees
Naira prices are approximate and vary.
12 members each care for 5 trees.
Seedlings cost about 300 naira each, so 60 cost about 18,000 naira.
After three months, 42 are alive. 42 divided by 60, times 100, is a 70% survival rate. Most losses were next to the football field, where children trampled them.
Replacing 18 trees costs about 5,400 naira. So they add stick rings on that side, and aim for at least 85% survival.
Safety first
Do
Talk to the LGA sanitation office first
Wear thick gloves and boots
Lift slabs with several people
Bag waste and arrange collection
Wash hands with soap afterwards
Never
Let children help in drains
Enter a drain when water is flowing
Burn the waste

In towns, much flooding happens because drains are blocked with plastic bags and bottles. Clear them before the heavy rains. Talk to your LGA sanitation office first. They may lend tools and collect the waste.
Wear thick gloves and boots, cover cuts, and wash your hands well with soap afterwards.
Never let children help in drains. Never enter a drain during rain or when water is flowing. And never burn the waste, because burning plastic gives off harmful smoke.
Talking about it
Zainab's ten-minute talk
What causes it, in three sentences
What it means here, plus one action
Questions
Zainab has ten minutes at her market women's meeting in Kaduna. She starts with what people have seen: who remembers when the rains started in April? This year we waited until May.
She explains the cause simply, then what it means in the market: hotter afternoons. She shows the heat danger signs.
After questions, she makes one clear ask: write your name here if you will check on one older trader in the next hot spell. Eleven members sign up.
If someone says it is just a bad year, do not argue. Say, let us check our records.
Partners
A request partners can say yes to
Who your group is, in one sentence
What you have already done, with numbers
Exactly what you need, and by when
What you will do in return
A contact name, and follow up in a week

Partners include the LGA, the State Ministry of Environment, extension workers, the health centre and NiMet. Make your request small and specific. For example, we planted 60 trees and 42 survived. Can your office supply 20 replacement seedlings before 15 May?
Be careful of anyone who asks your group to pay a fee for climate grants. Genuine agencies do not ask for payment through personal accounts.
Your capstone
Rahila's honest project summary
Practice: raised stock and a heat rota
Baseline: 2 baskets spoiled by flood water
After: no stock lost in 3 heavy rains
Rota: 96 of 108 checks made, about 89%
Income score: down from 9 to 7
Small and finished beats big and abandoned.
Rahila sells pepper and tomatoes in Lafia. Her top vulnerability was income. She raised her stock on a wooden platform and set up a heat rota for 9 older traders.
Before, she lost about 2 baskets to flood water. After, she lost none in 3 heavy rains.
The rota made 96 of 108 planned checks. She says honestly that the missed ones were on a market holiday, and how they fixed it.
When she rescored, her income score fell from 9 to 7.
